title: The Monitoring Paradox: Frontal Electroencephalography Reveals Profound Cortical Depression Despite Cardiovascular Stability in Dogs Undergoing Tibial Plateau Leveling Osteotomy
content: Frontal electroencephalography (EEG) and parasympathetic tone activity (PTA) are rarely used to assess anesthetic depth in dogs. This study evaluated whether these tools detect brain state changes missed by conventional cardiovascular monitoring. Twenty-one dogs undergoing tibial plateau leveling osteotomies received dexmedetomidine and hydromorphone premedication, propofol and ketamine induction, and isoflurane maintenance. Dogs were assigned to three analgesic protocols: intravenous fentanyl infusion, epidural morphine, or regional local blocks. While cardiovascular indices remained clinically acceptable across groups, EEG and PTA revealed a profound monitoring paradox. Autonomic vital signs frequently mask severe cortical depression. The fentanyl infusion group experienced the deepest and most consistent cortical suppression, yielding the highest incidence of Double-Low states (profound cortical suppression paired with low inhalant requirements). However, all evaluated protocols demonstrated the potential to decouple brainstem driven hemodynamic stability from cortical consciousness. Transitioning rapidly from deeply suppressed cortical states to wakefulness predisposed dogs to dysphoric recoveries. Ultimately, modern veterinary anesthesia requires integrating EEG and PTA monitoring alongside conventional cardiovascular assessment to optimize neurophysiological stability and improve postoperative outcomes.
